title: Hushwave throughput scratch
content:
Context: quick personal scratchpad for a focused microburst -> steady-state throughput experiment I ran on the small-model pool (g4dn-ish equivalent) with the hushwave ingress pattern (short-lived spikes at 200-300 qps, 95% requests are tiny - 8-16 tokens). Goal: understand the p95/p99 behavior and the interaction between KV cache priming, continuous batching, and the preemption policy on this fleet.

Summary of findings (high level):
- Warm-cache steady-state: p50 ~ 12ms, p95 ~ 32ms, p99 ~ 88ms at 220 qps with batch target 16
- Cold-cache microburst (first 30s after idle): large tail amplification — observed p99 spikes to 450-620ms correlated with tokenization + kv cache miss path
- Batching policy impact: increasing max_batch_size from 16->32 reduced p50 by ~10% but increased p99 by ~30% under microbursts (more queuing when a small number of long requests arrive)
- Preemptible evictions: when node eviction happened during a sustained surge (~5% of runs), tail jumped erratically (p99 > 1s) due to KV cache rehydration and GPU context warmup

Experimental setup (notes):
- Model: small-chat-1 (decoder-only, seq_len distribution: 85% <= 16 tokens, 15% 17-48 tokens)
- Fleet: 8 instances, each 1 GPU, 16 concurrency slots theoretical
- Traffic: hushwave pattern generator (python script) — 10s ramps every 60s: idle 30s -> spike to 220-300 qps for 20s -> decay 10s -> idle
- Runtime config variations tested:
  A) kv_cache: enabled vs disabled
  B) continuous_batching: target=8 / 16 / 32
  C) preemption_policy: soft (drain) vs immediate
  D) request_timeout_ms: 2000 vs 5000
- Observability: per-request trace id, tokenized_len tag, cache_hit boolean, batch_size when executed; aggregated by 1s buckets

Raw-ish numbers (representative run windows):
- Warm-cache window (kv_cache enabled, target=16): 60s steady at 220 qps
  - p50: 11.8ms
  - p95: 31.7ms
  - p99: 87.9ms
  - avg_batch_size: 12.6
  - kv_cache_hit_rate (prefix): 92%

- Cold microburst first spike (same config, first 30s after idle):
  - p50: 14.5ms
  - p95: 210ms
  - p99: 512ms (spike tail)
  - notable: 4 requests hit disk-backed cache path (kv miss) and each incurred ~220-320ms extra

- No-KV-cache run (target=16): spikes still present but p99 reduced to 320-380ms vs 512ms, p95 closer to 170ms. Explanation: removing KV cache avoids the expensive rehydration path but increases steady per-token compute slightly (p50 +2ms).

- Batch size sweep (kv_cache enabled):
  - target=8: steady p95 ~ 36ms, p99 ~ 110ms, avg_batch_size ~7.1
  - target=16: steady p95 ~ 32ms, p99 ~ 88ms, avg_batch_size ~12.6
  - target=32: steady p95 ~ 28ms, p99 ~ 115ms, avg_batch_size ~24.4
  Notes: larger batch lowers median and p95 due to throughput efficiency, but when a microburst contains many short requests, p99 can degrade because we wait to fill batches (even small delays amplify tails if the system holds out for more requests). Continuous batching heuristics that use max_delay_ms=2-4 help balance this.

- Preemption policy
  - soft drain: less p99 noise during scheduled node scaling events
  - immediate eviction: frequent p99 jumps > 900ms when eviction coincides with spikes. Root cause: eviction triggers GPU context tear down + KV cache loss on that node; requests routed to other nodes suffer spike from rehydration and queue reshuffle.

Interesting traces / debug observations:
- Trace 20241012-1348-0a2: chain where tokenization took 18ms, scheduler queued for 9ms, batch execution 6ms, then a cache-miss cold-load step 250ms (s3 fetch simulated) — this single outlier created long tail for the whole second.
- Trace 20241012-1412-3c9: preemption happened during spike; multiple inflight batches got redistributed and saw quadratic queuing (one node queued 6 batches while others drained) — we need better global backpressure signals.

Quick conclusions / heuristics to try next:
1) Improve KV cache priming: proactively prime likely prefixes for workloads with high diurnal gaps. Simple heuristics: prime on first request per client for 3 subsequent requests (staggered background priming).
2) Adaptive batching: reduce batch target dynamically during microburst onset (detect surge slope > X qps/s) to reduce p99; then ramp batch target back up in 3s.
3) Eviction coordination: make preemption graceful by pre-copying KV cache for recently hot keys to neighbors (or shared ephemeral cache), or mark nodes as unassignable but keep them serving until their warmup score decays
4) Request hedging: for tail-critical routes, send a shadow request to another node after 120ms if not started executing (dangerous cost-wise but useful for SLO experiments)
5) Investigate tokenization cost: seen 15-30ms variability on the tokenizer in cold path. Could memoize per-client tokenizer state for small vocab subsets used frequently.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- How much of the cold-path p99 is internal IO vs S3-like object fetch? (Some of our simulated KV rehydration uses remote object store; quantify by running a local in-process KV to isolate network factor)
- Can we model the surge slope detection with 95th-ordered exponential smoothing to avoid oscillation?
- Is the cost of hedging worth it for enterprise routes with 500ms p99 SLO? Run a cost vs latency simulation.

Next steps (short):
- Run a controlled A/B on quiet pool: local-kv (inproc) vs s3-kv to quantify network contribution (Mira)
- Implement simple surge detector -> batch_target adjustment in orchestrator (Kian)
- Add a synthetic priming job: after 20s idle, send 3 priming requests with stagger 50ms to simulate client fingerprints
- Record another 12h run overnight and capture heap/GPU memory graphs (I'll schedule)

Notes-to-self (random):
- Keep the hushwave generator idempotent; add a mode where 1% of requests intentionally request a long sequence (200 tokens) to test mixed-length tail interactions.
- Document the exact CPU/GPU kernel versions when I archive results. Suspect old cuBLAS kernels cause small jitter on large batches on this infra.
- If we do hedging, add a budget meter at route level (hedge_tokens_allowed/day) and expose in console.

Appendix: quick command snippets used (for reproducibility)
- generator start: python bench/hushwave_gen.py --qps 220 --pattern hushwave --seed 20241012 --clients 80
- collect traces: curl "http://obs:9200/trace/_search?q=run:hushwave-20241012&size=1000" > traces.json
- batch policy tweak: curl -X POST http://orchestrator/api/v1/config -d '{"route":"small-chat-1","batch_target":16}'

End of scratch. Save a cleaner version to Confluence if any of the heuristics make it to a PR.
